title: Tongues, Prophecy, and Order in Worship
summary: Paul compares speaking in tongues with prophecy and argues that in the gathered church intelligible speech that builds others up is better than uninterpreted tongues. He gives practical rules: tongues only with interpretation, two or three speakers at a time, prophecies weighed by others, and everything done in a fitting and orderly way. The chapter also includes a debated instruction for women to be silent in the churches.
story: This chapter completes Paul's answer about spiritual gifts (chapters 12 to 14). Chapter 12 showed that the Spirit gives many gifts for the common good; chapter 13 showed that love is the only right way to use them. Now Paul applies both to the specific problem at Corinth: gatherings dominated by uninterpreted tongues, many people speaking at once, and outsiders left bewildered. His test throughout is the one love supplies: does this build up the church? After this chapter the letter turns to its last great theme, the resurrection (chapter 15), which is also the hope toward which the partial gifts point.
historical:
Corinthian worship took place in homes, probably with a few dozen people, and included a meal (chapter 11), singing, teaching, prayer, prophecy, and tongues. Participation was open and spontaneous: “everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation” (verse 26). No fixed liturgy or appointed preacher is mentioned. Visitors could walk in, including “uninstructed” people (probably inquirers or new believers) and unbelievers (verses 23 and 24).

In verse 21 Paul quotes Isaiah 28:11-12, where God warned Israel that because they refused his clear word through the prophets, he would speak to them through the foreign tongue of Assyrian invaders, a sign of judgment. Paul applies the passage to show that tongues without interpretation function as a sign of judgment on unbelievers, not as a means of winning them (verse 22).
cultural:
Greek religion knew inspired speech. The prophetess at Delphi delivered oracles in a state of possession that priests then interpreted, and ecstatic cults prized frenzy as evidence of a god's presence. Paul's instructions distinguish Christian prophecy and tongues from that model: “The spirits of prophets are subject to prophets” (verse 32). The speaker remains in control and can stop, wait a turn, or keep silent.

In a society governed by honor and shame, public speech was also shaped by social expectations. Women in Greco-Roman society were generally expected not to speak publicly in mixed assemblies, and questioning another woman's husband or a male teacher in public could be seen as shameful. Education was unequal, so many women would have had fewer opportunities to learn than men. These customs are part of the background of verses 34 and 35, although interpreters weigh them differently.
literary: The argument alternates between comparison, analogy, and instruction. Paul contrasts tongues (speaking to God, building up oneself) with prophecy (speaking to people, building up the church) in verses 1 to 5, then illustrates with musical instruments, a trumpet in battle, and foreign languages (verses 6 to 12). He speaks personally in verses 14 to 19 (“I thank God that I speak in tongues more than all of you”), which prevents readers from thinking he despises the gift. The word “build up” (edify) and its noun recur throughout. The practical rules of verses 26 to 33 are followed by the disputed verses 34 and 35, then a sharp rhetorical challenge (verse 36), a claim to speak the Lord's command (verse 37), and a balanced summary (verses 39 and 40).

outline.t: Prophecy builds up the church more than tongues
Unintelligible sound does not help anyone
Pray with the spirit and with the mind
Orderly worship: turns, interpretation, and weighing
Women to be silent in the churches
The Lord's command: eagerness with order

doctrines.note: The gathered church exists to be built up: “All of these must be done to build up the church” (verse 26). Worship is participatory, and every contribution is judged by whether it helps others understand, grow, and be encouraged.

The Spirit does not override the person. Prophets are in control of their own spirits (verse 32), and God “is not a God of disorder, but of peace” (verse 33). True spiritual power produces order and understanding, not chaos.

Prophecy in this chapter is Spirit-given speech that must be weighed (verse 29) and that reveals the secrets of hearts (verse 25). Christians differ over how New Testament prophecy relates to Scripture, whether it continues today, and whether it carries the same authority, but Paul clearly subjects it to testing and to the apostolic word (verse 37).

words.note: Oikodome, building up or edification, literally the act of building a house. It is the key word of the chapter. The Corinthians wanted gifts that displayed their spirituality; Paul wants gifts that build up others. Edification is the test that love applies to worship.

Propheteuo, to prophesy. In the New Testament it means speaking a message prompted by the Spirit, which may include encouragement, comfort, conviction, or revelation of hidden things (verses 3 and 25). It is not mainly foretelling the future. Paul values it because it is intelligible and builds others up.

Glossa, tongue or language, used fifteen times here. Interpreters debate whether Corinthian tongues were unlearned human languages, as at Pentecost (Acts 2), or a heavenly or ecstatic form of prayer (compare the “tongues of men and of angels” in 13:1). Paul says the speaker addresses God, speaks mysteries, and needs interpretation for others to understand (verses 2 and 13).

Sigao, to be silent, used three times: for the tongues-speaker without an interpreter (verse 28), for a prophet when another receives a revelation (verse 30), and for women (verse 34). How the three silences relate to one another is part of the debate over verses 34 and 35.

christ: The chapter shows Christ at work through his Spirit in the gathered church. When prophecy lays bare an outsider's heart, he falls down and confesses, “God is truly among you” (verse 25), echoing Isaiah 45:14, where the nations acknowledge Israel's God. The risen Christ is present among his people by the Spirit, and his presence should be recognizable to outsiders. Paul also claims that what he writes is “the Lord's command” (verse 37), meaning the authority of Christ stands behind his apostolic instruction. And the chapter's concern for the weak, the uninstructed, and the outsider reflects the self-giving love of Christ described in chapter 13.

hard.q: What does Paul mean when he says “Women are to be silent in the churches,” when in 11:5 he assumes women pray and prophesy aloud?
hard.a:
There is first a textual question. Every known manuscript contains verses 34 and 35, but in a few, mostly from the Western tradition, they appear after verse 40 instead. Some scholars, notably Gordon Fee, have argued that the verses were an early marginal note later inserted into the text; most scholars hold that they are original and that the displacement was a scribal attempt to smooth the flow.

Among those who take the verses as Paul's, the main readings are these. Some hold that Paul forbids women to take part in the public weighing or judging of prophecies (verse 29), a role involving authoritative teaching, while allowing them to pray and prophesy; this reading is common among complementarians. Others think Paul addresses disruptive questioning or chatter during worship by women who had less education, and his remedy is that they ask at home (verse 35); this reading, common among egalitarians, sees a local problem of order, like the silences imposed on tongues-speakers and prophets in the same passage. A few take verses 34 and 35 as a Corinthian view that Paul quotes and then rejects in verse 36, though the Greek gives no clear signal of a quotation. Historically, some churches have read the verses as a general rule forbidding women to speak in the assembly, though few practiced total silence given 11:5. Readers also debate whether “as the law says” refers to Genesis, to the Old Testament in general, or to common custom, since no Old Testament text commands women's silence. These are second-order questions on which faithful churches differ, and each view tries to honor both 11:5 and 14:34.

questions: Paul would rather speak five words that others understand than ten thousand they do not. How could your church's gatherings become clearer and more helpful to newcomers?
What does it look like for worship to be both Spirit-filled and orderly? Do you tend to value one more than the other?
How do you read a difficult passage like verses 34 and 35 when faithful Christians disagree about it?
